assessment.nobel_worthiness: Information design supplies a fundamental framework for analyzing how strategically chosen information changes economic outcomes, with wide relevance to markets, institutions and policy.
assessment.attribution: Bergemann, Kamenica and Morris are central architects of the theoretical foundations; Gentzkow is an important contributor to applications and related work.
assessment.maturity: The framework is sufficiently established to have generated a large and still expanding body of theoretical and applied research.
uncertainties: The appropriate division between foundational information-design work and later applications remains contestable.
Its ultimate practical influence relative to its theoretical influence is still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Network economics has changed how economists model interaction, diffusion, externalities and strategic behavior when economic relationships are endogenous.
assessment.attribution: Jackson and Goyal are especially central to the formal economic analysis of networks, while Kranton made major contributions linking networks to economic incentives and organization.
assessment.maturity: The field has matured into a durable research program with broad connections across theory, empirical work and policy-relevant questions.
uncertainties: The contribution is diffuse across a broad literature, making a three-person attribution inherently incomplete.
Evidence on the quantitative importance of particular network mechanisms varies by setting.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The analysis of ambiguity gave economics rigorous alternatives to expected utility for decisions in which probabilities themselves are uncertain.
assessment.attribution: Gilboa and Epstein provide distinct foundational approaches, and Marinacci is a major contributor to axiomatization and development of ambiguity theory.
assessment.maturity: These models are long established and have influenced decision theory, finance, macroeconomics and mechanism design.
uncertainties: The contribution comprises related but distinct models rather than one singular discovery.
The relative claim of other foundational contributors to ambiguity theory requires careful resolution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Alternating-offer bargaining and its extensions provided a canonical strategic account of bargaining outcomes and market frictions.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein is the indispensable originator of the alternating-offers model; Wolinsky and Binmore made important contributions to bargaining theory and its economic interpretation.
assessment.maturity: The core model is exceptionally mature, canonical and deeply embedded in economic theory.
uncertainties: Rubinstein's foundational contribution is substantially more sharply identified than the proposed joint attribution.
The empirical realism of bargaining protocols and bargaining power assumptions is context dependent.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification transformed econometric practice by showing what conclusions are warranted when conventional identifying assumptions cannot be defended.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the central intellectual founder, with Tamer and Molinari making major advances in moment inequalities and inference for partially identified models.
assessment.maturity: The approach has become a durable part of modern econometrics and a practical discipline of transparent inference.
uncertainties: The breadth of the surrounding identification literature makes exact credit allocation difficult.
The approach sometimes yields wide bounds, limiting direct policy resolution in specific applications.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic discrete-choice methods made it possible to estimate forward-looking behavior structurally and have shaped work in labor, industrial organization and public economics.
assessment.attribution: Rust supplied the seminal computational and econometric framework, while Keane and Eckstein made major methodological and applied contributions.
assessment.maturity: The methods have been tested and elaborated over decades and remain central despite substantial computational evolution.
uncertainties: Rust's priority is clearer than the case for a three-person prize.
Structural estimates remain sensitive to modeling assumptions and specification choices.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Research on reciprocity, fairness and inequity aversion substantially broadened economic models of motivation and improved their explanatory reach.
assessment.attribution: Fehr is a leading architect of the experimental and theoretical program; Falk and Schmidt made central complementary contributions.
assessment.maturity: The core findings and models have endured extensive experimental, theoretical and applied engagement.
uncertainties: The evidence spans heterogeneous laboratory and field settings, with unresolved questions about external validity.
Credit extends beyond the listed trio to a broad behavioral-economics literature.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The joint theoretical and empirical study of insurance selection has clarified the welfare and design consequences of asymmetric information in major real-world markets.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein and Einav are central empirical contributors, while Salanie has made important theoretical and econometric contributions to selection analysis.
assessment.maturity: The research agenda has produced influential evidence across insurance markets and has clear implications for market design and public policy.
uncertainties: The candidate bundle combines several related empirical and theoretical strands rather than a single sharply bounded discovery.
Policy implications depend on institutional details and on the coexistence of moral hazard with selection.
